subject: Kemi
title: Materials, metals and cycles
sourceSummary: The properties of metals and where they come from, how recycling and material cycles work, common everyday materials such as plastic, glass and metal, and the basic idea behind corrosion and rust.

questions.prompt: Which property is typical of metals but NOT of most other materials?
questions.opener: Think about why you can conduct electricity and heat through a metal cable or a saucepan.
choices: They dissolve easily in water
They conduct electricity and heat well
They are transparent
They are always soft and flexible
questions.explanation: Metals conduct electricity and heat well thanks to free electrons that can move through the material. They are usually not transparent, do not dissolve in water, and vary greatly in hardness — iron is hard while lead is soft.

questions.prompt: Where in nature are most metals found before they are mined and extracted?
questions.opener: Pure metals are rare in nature — they are usually bound to other substances.
choices: Free in the air as a gas
Bound in ore together with other elements, for example oxygen
Dissolved in seawater in large quantities
They are only formed in factories
questions.explanation: Most metals are found in nature bound in ore, often together with oxygen as metal oxides. To obtain pure metal, the ore must be mined and then processed, for example by smelting.

questions.prompt: Why is it particularly good for the environment to recycle metals such as aluminium?
questions.opener: Compare the energy it takes to mine new ore and smelt new metal with melting down scrap.
choices: Metals can only be recycled once
It takes much less energy to melt down scrap than to extract new metal from ore
Recycled metal is always stronger than new metal
Metals break down naturally if you throw them out in nature
questions.explanation: Melting down scrap metal requires considerably less energy than mining ore and extracting new metal from scratch, which saves both energy and natural resources. Metals can also be recycled again and again without losing their properties.

questions.prompt: What is meant by a material cycle?
questions.opener: Think about the difference between a material being used once and thrown away, and it being used again and again.
choices: That material is manufactured once and then always thrown away in nature
That material is collected, processed and used to make new products again and again, instead of becoming waste
That material can only ever be used to make exactly the same product as before
Another word for the rubbish dump
questions.explanation: A material cycle means that material is collected after use, processed and turned into raw material for new products, instead of becoming waste that is thrown away. This saves raw materials and energy compared with always manufacturing new material from scratch.

questions.prompt: What is the most important chemical difference between plastic and glass?
questions.opener: Think about what the substances are built from at the molecular level — long chains compared with a network of silicon dioxide.
choices: Plastic is always transparent and glass never is
Plastic consists of long chains of carbon atoms (polymers), while glass mainly consists of silicon dioxide in a hard network
Glass always contains metal and plastic never does
There is no chemical difference, only a difference in appearance
questions.explanation: Plastic is built up of polymers — long chains of carbon atoms that make the material mouldable. Glass, on the other hand, mainly consists of silicon dioxide (the same substance found in sand), which forms a hard, rigid network as it solidifies from its molten form.

questions.opener: Think about which substances in the air react with iron over time.
choices: Pure iron metal that has simply changed colour
An iron oxide compound that forms when iron reacts with oxygen and moisture
Dirt that has stuck to the surface of the iron from outside
Another name for aluminium oxide
questions.explanation: Rust is iron oxide (actually a mixture of iron oxides and iron hydroxides) that forms when iron slowly reacts with oxygen and water in the air. Rust is therefore not the same substance as the iron itself, but an entirely new chemical compound — corrosion is a chemical reaction, not just dirt.

questions.prompt: Explain why an iron nail rusts when left out in the rain, but a stainless steel nail does not do so as easily.
questions.opener: Think about what iron needs in order to rust, and what chemically distinguishes stainless steel from ordinary iron.
questions.answer: The iron nail rusts because pure iron reacts directly with oxygen and moisture and forms iron oxide. Stainless steel contains chromium, which forms a thin, invisible protective oxide layer on the surface that prevents oxygen and moisture from reaching the iron underneath.
steps: Rust forms through a chemical reaction between iron, oxygen (from the air) and water (from the rain).
A bare iron surface has no protection, so the reaction can continue for as long as the surface is exposed, and the rust builds up layer by layer.
Stainless steel is an alloy of iron with, among other things, chromium added.
The chromium reacts quickly with oxygen and forms a very thin, tight chromium oxide layer that 'covers' the surface.
That layer prevents oxygen and moisture from reaching the iron underneath, so the usual rust attack is avoided or proceeds much more slowly.

questions.prompt: Summarise the key points about metals, common everyday materials and recycling.
questions.opener: Think through where metals come from, what distinguishes plastic/glass/metal, and why recycling pays off.
questions.answer: Metals: conduct electricity and heat well, are usually shiny and mouldable, are found in nature bound in ore and must be extracted · Alloy = a mixture of a metal with other substances for new properties, e.g. stainless steel (iron + chromium) · Plastic: built from long carbon chains (polymers), light and mouldable, breaks down very slowly in nature · Glass: mainly silicon dioxide, hard and transparent but brittle · Corrosion/rust: iron reacts with oxygen and moisture and forms iron oxide — a chemical reaction, not just dirt · Material cycle = material is collected, processed and turned into raw material for new products instead of becoming waste · Recycling metal (e.g. aluminium) requires much less energy than extracting new metal from ore.

questions.prompt: What is a mixture of a metal with one or more other substances called, made to give new properties, for example stainless steel?
questions.opener: Iron mixed with chromium is a classic example.
choices: An alloy
An ion
A hydrocarbon
A polymer
questions.explanation: An alloy is a mixture of a metal with one or more other substances, giving the material new properties - stainless steel is iron alloyed with, among other things, chromium.

questions.prompt: Why do metals conduct electricity well?
questions.opener: Think about what allows charge to move through the material.
choices: They have free electrons that can move through the material
They contain a lot of water
They are always magnetic
They have low density
questions.explanation: The metallic bond means electrons move freely throughout the material, which allows electric charge to be carried - this is the basis of metals' good conductivity.

questions.prompt: What is an advantage of metals being recyclable again and again, unlike some other materials?
questions.opener: Think about whether the metal's properties change after it's melted down.
choices: The metal's properties don't change even after several recycling cycles
Metals can only be recycled once
Recycling metal requires more energy than extracting new metal
Recycled metal can never be used for new products
questions.explanation: Metal can be melted down and reused again and again without losing its basic properties, which makes recycling especially valuable compared with materials that degrade when recycled.

questions.prompt: What do plastic, glass and metal have in common despite their different chemical structures?
questions.opener: Think broadly - what do people do with all three materials?
choices: They are all materials people use and process for various everyday purposes
They are all made of polymers
They all conduct electricity equally well
They all break down at the same rate in nature
questions.explanation: Despite completely different chemical structures (polymers, a silicon dioxide network, and metallic bonding respectively), all three are used as everyday materials, chosen for their respective properties.

questions.prompt: What is required for iron to rust?
questions.opener: Two substances in the air and weather both need to be present.
choices: Oxygen and moisture (water)
Only high temperature
Only sunlight
Nitrogen and carbon dioxide
questions.explanation: Rust forms when iron reacts with both oxygen and water (moisture) at the same time - if either is missing, rust formation is much slower or doesn't happen at all.

questions.prompt: Explain why it's more energy-efficient to recycle aluminium cans than to manufacture new aluminium cans from ore (bauxite), and what that means for the environment.
questions.opener: Compare what's needed to break chemical bonds in ore with what's needed to simply remelt pure metal.
questions.answer: Extracting aluminium from ore requires very energy-intensive processes to break down the strong chemical bonds, while remelting already-pure aluminium metal only requires heating the metal to its melting point - which saves a large share of the energy.
steps: Aluminium in ore (bauxite) is tightly bound to oxygen as aluminium oxide, and breaking these bonds requires a lot of energy, often through electrolysis.
Remelting already-extracted, pure aluminium metal only requires heating the metal to its melting point - no new strong chemical bond needs to be broken.
This makes recycling aluminium far less energy-intensive than producing it new.
Less energy use means lower greenhouse gas emissions and less need to mine new ore, which spares natural resources and the environment.

questions.prompt: Why are iron bridges and other outdoor iron structures often painted?
questions.opener: Think about what rust formation requires, and what the paint blocks.
choices: The paint creates a protective layer that blocks oxygen and moisture from reaching the iron, slowing down rust formation
Painting makes the iron mechanically stronger
Painting prevents the iron from conducting electricity
Painting has no practical function, only an aesthetic one
questions.explanation: The paint layer acts as a barrier that blocks oxygen and moisture from reaching the iron surface, greatly slowing the chemical reaction that causes rust - the same principle as the chromium layer in stainless steel.
